process.title: Login or session handling of [name] can be bypassed or brute-forced
process.desc: Weak authentication — no limit on login attempts, sessions that never expire, guessable tokens or a flawed password-reset flow — lets attackers log in as real users.
controls: Use a proven identity provider or framework instead of custom login code
Rate-limit and monitor failed logins
Short-lived sessions, rotated on login and privilege change
Secure, single-use password-reset tokens

process.title: Forged or tampered tokens accepted by [name]
process.desc: Tokens (JWT, SAML, API keys) are accepted without fully checking the signature, signing key, issuer, audience and expiry, so attackers can mint their own tokens.
controls: Validate signature with an allow-list of algorithms and keys
Check issuer, audience, expiry and not-before on every request
Rotate signing keys and keep them in a vault/HSM
process.example: Storm-0558 (2023): a stolen Microsoft consumer signing key was accepted for enterprise tokens because of a validation flaw, giving access to email at about 25 organizations.

process.title: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) against [name]
process.desc: The browser automatically sends the user's cookies, so a malicious site can make a signed-in user's browser perform actions (change email, transfer money) without their intent.
controls: SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies
Anti-CSRF tokens for state-changing requests
Check the Origin header; never change state on GET

process.title: Unauthenticated callers reach [name]
process.desc: A component that handles sensitive data or is business-critical accepts requests that are not authenticated, so anyone who can reach it can use it.
controls: Authenticate every inbound request (OAuth2/OIDC, mTLS between services)
Deny by default at the gateway
Inventory endpoints so test or legacy APIs are not left open
process.example: Optus (2022): a customer API reachable from the internet without authentication — attributed by the regulator to an access-control coding error — exposed data of about 9.8 million people.

process.title: Injection (SQL, NoSQL, OS command, template) in [name]
process.desc: User-controlled input is built into a query, command or template, letting an attacker read or change data or run commands with the service's rights.
controls: Parameterised queries / ORM; never concatenate input
Avoid shell calls; pass arguments as arrays
Allow-list validation on input
Least-privilege database and OS accounts
process.example: MOVEit Transfer (2023, CVE-2023-34362): an unauthenticated SQL injection was used for mass data theft from thousands of organizations.

process.title: Mass assignment lets users change protected fields
process.desc: The API binds the whole request body to an object, so a user can set fields they should not control — role, price, owner, verification status.
controls: Explicit allow-lists (DTOs) for writable fields
Separate read and write models
Server-side authorization per field

process.title: Race conditions in business transactions
process.desc: Concurrent requests exploit check-then-act gaps: a coupon used twice, a balance withdrawn twice, stock oversold.
controls: Database transactions with row locks or atomic updates
Idempotency keys on payment and order APIs
Unique constraints for one-time actions

process.title: Path traversal or malicious file upload
process.desc: File names like ../../etc/passwd or uploaded scripts let attackers read or overwrite files, or run code on the server.
controls: Generate server-side file names; never use user paths
Store uploads outside the web root, on separate storage
Check type by content, limit size, scan for malware

process.title: Data from third-party APIs is trusted without validation
process.desc: Responses from partners or external APIs are used as if they were safe — following their redirects, storing their HTML, passing their values into queries.
controls: Validate and sanitise third-party data like user input
Use TLS and verify certificates for outgoing calls
Timeouts and limits on responses; do not follow redirects blindly

process.title: Compromised dependency or build pipeline ships malicious code in [name]
process.desc: A malicious package, a hijacked maintainer account or a tampered build system inserts a backdoor into what you deploy, signed as your own software.
controls: Pin dependency versions and verify checksums/signatures
Protect CI/CD: least-privilege tokens, protected branches, reviewed pipeline changes
SBOM, dependency scanning, private package mirror
process.example: SolarWinds (2020): attackers modified the build system so that signed Orion updates contained the SUNBURST backdoor. xz Utils (2024, CVE-2024-3094): a backdoor inserted by a co-maintainer who had built trust over about two years.

process.title: Security events in [name] are not logged
process.desc: Logins, failed access checks, permission changes and access to sensitive records are not recorded with who, what, when and from where, so misuse cannot be detected or proven.
controls: Log security events with user, action, target, time and source IP
Ship logs to a central store the service cannot modify
Alert on suspicious patterns (many failures, privilege changes)

process.title: Log injection forges or hides log entries
process.desc: User input is written to logs unchanged, so newlines and control characters create fake entries or break log parsing and alerting.
controls: Structured (JSON) logging
Encode or strip control characters from logged values

process.title: An attacker on [name] can delete or alter its logs
process.desc: Logs are only stored where the compromised service or host can modify them, so the first thing an attacker does is erase their tracks.
controls: Forward logs in real time to a separate, append-only store
Alert when log forwarding stops

process.title: Broken object-level authorization (IDOR) in [name]
process.desc: The service returns or changes a record when the caller supplies its ID, without checking that the caller is allowed to access that particular record.
controls: Check ownership/permission for every object access, server-side
Use unguessable IDs as defence in depth (not as the control)
Automated tests that request other users' objects
process.example: First American Financial (2019): changing a number in a document URL exposed about 885 million mortgage records without any login.

process.title: API responses expose more data than the client needs
process.desc: Endpoints return full objects (internal IDs, emails, flags, other users' fields) and rely on the front-end to hide them.
controls: Explicit response schemas per endpoint
Never return internal or other users' fields
Review API responses in code review and tests

process.title: Secrets hard-coded in code, scripts, images or config of [name]
process.desc: Passwords, API keys and private keys committed to repositories or baked into images and scripts can be read by anyone with access to those artefacts.
controls: Keep secrets in a vault/secret manager and inject at runtime
Secret scanning in CI and on repositories
Rotate any secret that was ever committed
process.example: Uber (2022): an attacker found admin credentials for the company's privileged-access system in a PowerShell script on a network share. Toyota (2022): an access key sat in a public GitHub repository for about five years.

process.title: Sensitive data written to logs, traces or diagnostic files
process.desc: Tokens, passwords, personal data or full request bodies end up in logs, traces, crash reports or support uploads, which many more people and systems can read.
controls: Redact secrets and personal data before logging
Never log Authorization headers, cookies or full bodies
Restrict and expire access to logs and diagnostic files
process.example: Okta (2023): HAR files uploaded to the support system contained session tokens that attackers used to hijack customer sessions.

process.title: Error messages reveal internal details
process.desc: Stack traces, SQL errors and version strings in responses give attackers a map of the system for further attacks.
controls: Generic error responses to clients; details only in server logs
Disable debug mode in production

process.title: Personalised responses cached and served to other users
process.desc: A CDN or reverse proxy caches pages or API responses that contain one user's data and serves them to others.
controls: Cache-Control: private/no-store on personalised responses
Cache keys that include the user or vary correctly
Test caching rules after CDN changes
process.example: Steam (December 2015): a caching misconfiguration during a traffic spike showed users other people's account pages.

process.title: Secrets exposed in crash dumps or memory snapshots
process.desc: Keys and tokens held in memory end up in core dumps, heap snapshots or debug captures that are copied to less-protected environments.
controls: Keep signing keys in an HSM or managed key service
Disable or scrub crash dumps in production
Treat debug environments as sensitive
process.example: Storm-0558 (2023): the stolen signing key had ended up in a crash dump that was moved to a debugging environment.

process.title: Unrestricted resource consumption in [name]
process.desc: Missing limits on request rate, payload size, page size or expensive operations let one client exhaust CPU, memory, connections or paid third-party quotas.
controls: Rate limits and quotas per client
Limits on payload, page and batch sizes
Timeouts and bounded worker pools

process.title: Small requests trigger very expensive work (ReDoS, decompression bombs)
process.desc: Crafted input makes a regular expression, parser or decompressor do enormous amounts of work, pinning the CPU or filling memory.
controls: Linear-time regex engines or timeouts
Limits on decompressed size and nesting depth
Input length limits

process.title: Attackers run up the cloud or third-party bill of [name]
process.desc: Autoscaling, serverless functions and paid APIs (SMS, email, AI models) keep serving abusive traffic, turning an attack into a large invoice.
controls: Budgets and billing alerts
Per-user quotas on paid actions (SMS, AI calls)
Caps on autoscaling

process.title: Missing function-level authorization in [name]
process.desc: Administrative or privileged functions are reachable by normal users because the check is only done in the UI or not at all.
controls: Deny by default; central authorization for every endpoint
Separate admin APIs and tests that call them as a normal user

process.title: Server-side request forgery (SSRF) in [name]
process.desc: The service fetches URLs chosen by the user, so attackers make it call internal systems or the cloud metadata endpoint with its network position and credentials.
controls: Allow-list destinations; block private and metadata IP ranges
Use a separate egress proxy
Require IMDSv2 / metadata protection on cloud hosts
process.example: Capital One (2019): SSRF via a misconfigured WAF reached the EC2 metadata service, whose over-privileged role could read S3 buckets with data on about 100 million people.

process.title: Known-vulnerable component allows remote code execution in [name]
process.desc: An unpatched framework, library or server with a public exploit lets attackers run code inside the service.
controls: Dependency and image scanning with a patch SLA
Inventory of components (SBOM)
WAF/virtual patching while updating
process.example: Equifax (2017): an unpatched Apache Struts flaw (CVE-2017-5638). Log4Shell (2021, CVE-2021-44228): remote code execution through a logging library.

process.title: Insecure deserialization of untrusted data
process.desc: Turning untrusted bytes into native objects can execute code or bypass checks.
controls: Never deserialize untrusted native objects; use JSON with schema validation
Allow-list types if native formats are unavoidable

process.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS) in [name]
process.desc: Untrusted content is rendered as HTML or script, so attackers run code in other users' browsers with their session.
controls: Context-aware output encoding; framework auto-escaping
Content-Security-Policy
HttpOnly cookies

process.title: Compromise of [name] gives administrator control
process.desc: The component runs with administrative or root rights, so any code-execution flaw becomes full control of the host.
controls: Run as a dedicated least-privileged account
Drop capabilities; read-only file system; containers/sandboxing

process.title: Over-privileged service identity of [name]
process.desc: The cloud role, service account or database user used by the service can do far more than it needs, so one flaw exposes everything that identity can reach.
controls: Least-privilege roles per service, reviewed regularly
Separate identities per environment and function
Alert on unusual use of service identities
process.example: Capital One (2019): the role available to the compromised server could list and read many S3 buckets.

process.title: Crown jewel [name] is reachable from a less-trusted zone
process.desc: A business-critical component accepts traffic that crosses a trust boundary, so it is directly exposed to attacks from that zone.
controls: Put a gateway or proxy in front and expose only needed operations
Strict input validation and authorization at the boundary
Network segmentation

process.title: Prompt injection changes what [name] does
process.desc: Instructions hidden in user input, documents, web pages or emails processed by the model override the system prompt, making it ignore rules, leak data or misuse its tools.
controls: Treat all model input as untrusted; keep instructions and data separate
Least-privilege tools and human approval for impactful actions
Filter and monitor outputs; red-team with injection test sets

process.title: [name] reveals sensitive data from prompts, context or training data
process.desc: The model repeats personal data, secrets or other users' content from its context window, retrieved documents or fine-tuning data.
controls: Do not put secrets in prompts or context
Per-user authorization on retrieved documents (RAG)
Redact personal data before indexing or fine-tuning

process.title: Excessive agency: [name] takes harmful actions through its tools
process.desc: An LLM agent can call APIs, run code, send email or change data with broad permissions, so a manipulated or mistaken model acts with those rights.
controls: Give tools the minimum permissions and scope
Require confirmation for state-changing actions
Rate-limit and log every tool call

process.title: Model output from [name] used unsafely (XSS, SQL, shell)
process.desc: Text generated by the model is inserted into web pages, queries or commands without validation, turning prompt injection into classic injection.
controls: Encode model output for its destination; never execute it directly
Validate against schemas for structured output

process.title: System prompt of [name] can be extracted
process.desc: Users can make the model reveal its hidden instructions, exposing business rules, filters and any credentials or internal details placed there.
controls: Assume the system prompt is public; keep secrets and authorization logic out of it
Enforce rules outside the model
process.example: Bing Chat (February 2023): users made the assistant reveal its confidential instructions and internal code name.

process.title: Unbounded model usage makes [name] slow or expensive
process.desc: Long prompts, large outputs or automated querying consume GPU capacity and paid tokens, causing outages or large bills.
controls: Per-user quotas, input/output token limits and timeouts
Budget alerts on model usage

process.title: Price or amount in [name] can be changed by the client
process.desc: The server trusts price, discount, currency or quantity values sent by the browser or app, so users pay less than they should.
controls: Recalculate amounts server-side from the catalogue/order
Sign or look up amounts when calling the payment provider

process.title: Card data processed by [name] leaks into logs or storage
process.desc: Full card numbers or CVV end up in logs, analytics, error reports or the database, bringing the whole system into PCI DSS scope and exposing cardholder data.
controls: Use the payment provider's hosted fields/tokenisation so card data never touches your servers
Mask card numbers in logs; never store CVV

process.title: Card testing (carding) through [name]
process.desc: Fraudsters use the checkout to test large numbers of stolen cards with small payments, causing chargebacks, fees and provider sanctions.
controls: Bot detection and rate limits on payment attempts
3-D Secure / risk scoring from the provider
Alert on spikes in declined payments

process.title: Deeply nested or batched GraphQL queries overload [name]
process.desc: A single query with deep nesting, aliases or batching makes the server resolve millions of fields.
controls: Query depth, complexity and cost limits
Limit batching and aliases; persisted queries for public clients

process.title: GraphQL introspection exposes the full schema of [name]
process.desc: Introspection and field suggestions reveal every type, field and mutation, including internal and unfinished ones.
controls: Disable introspection and field suggestions in production
Authorization on every field and mutation, not only on the endpoint

process.title: CORS policy of [name] lets other websites read responses
process.desc: Reflecting any Origin, or allowing "null" or wildcard origins together with credentials, lets a malicious site read signed-in users' data.
controls: Explicit allow-list of origins
Never combine Access-Control-Allow-Credentials with wildcard or reflected origins

process.title: Open redirect in [name] used for phishing or token theft
process.desc: A redirect parameter accepts any URL, so links on your trusted domain send users to attacker sites or leak OAuth codes.
controls: Allow-list redirect targets or use relative paths only
Exact redirect URI matching for OAuth

process.title: Clickjacking against [name]
process.desc: The site can be framed by another page that tricks users into clicking buttons (approve, delete, transfer) they cannot see.
controls: Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors (or X-Frame-Options)
Confirmation for sensitive actions

process.title: OAuth/OIDC flow of [name] lets attackers steal codes or tokens
process.desc: Loose redirect URI matching, missing state/PKCE or the implicit flow let attackers intercept authorization codes or tokens.
controls: Exact redirect URI matching; PKCE for all clients
Validate state/nonce; no implicit flow
Short-lived, audience-restricted tokens

process.title: Forged SAML assertions accepted by [name]
process.desc: Unsigned assertions, signature-wrapping flaws or a stolen token-signing certificate let attackers log in as anyone.
controls: Validate signatures with a maintained library; reject unsigned assertions
Protect and monitor the token-signing certificate (HSM)
Alert on logins without matching IdP events
process.example: SolarWinds campaign (2020): attackers forged SAML tokens ("Golden SAML") with a stolen signing certificate to access cloud email.

process.title: Poisoned pipeline execution in [name]
process.desc: Pull requests, build scripts or third-party actions run attacker-controlled code inside the pipeline, which has access to secrets and deployment rights.
controls: Do not run untrusted pull requests with secrets
Pin third-party actions to commit SHAs
Separate build and deploy permissions
process.example: tj-actions/changed-files (2025, CVE-2025-30066): a compromised GitHub Action dumped CI secrets into build logs of thousands of repositories.

process.title: Secrets in [name] exposed through logs, forks or over-scoped tokens
process.desc: Pipeline secrets are printed to logs, available to forked builds, or are long-lived tokens with broad scopes.
controls: Short-lived OIDC credentials instead of stored cloud keys
Mask secrets in logs; scope tokens per job
Rotate secrets after incidents
process.example: CircleCI (2023): malware on an engineer's laptop stole an MFA-backed session; customers had to rotate all secrets stored in the platform.

process.title: Dependency confusion or typosquatting pulls malicious packages into [name]
process.desc: Package managers fetch a public package with the same or a similar name as an internal one, running attacker code during the build.
controls: Scoped/namespaced internal packages and a single private registry
Lock files with integrity hashes
Block install scripts where possible
process.example: Dependency confusion (2021): a researcher got code executed inside dozens of large companies, including Apple and Microsoft, by publishing public packages named like their internal ones.

process.title: Event injection into [name]
process.desc: Functions triggered by queues, storage uploads or webhooks trust event content (file names, metadata, message bodies) that attackers can control.
controls: Validate every event field like user input
Restrict who can publish events or upload files that trigger functions

process.title: Poison messages crash [name] repeatedly
process.desc: A malformed or oversized message makes the consumer fail, get redelivered and fail again, blocking all following messages.
controls: Dead-letter queues with retry limits
Schema validation and size limits before processing

process.title: Emails can be sent pretending to come from your domain
process.desc: Without SPF, DKIM and an enforcing DMARC policy, attackers send phishing or fake invoices that appear to come from you.
controls: SPF and DKIM for all sending services
DMARC with p=reject after monitoring

process.title: Email header injection through [name]
process.desc: User input placed in email headers (subject, to, reply-to) adds recipients or rewrites messages sent from your system.
controls: Strip CR/LF from header values; use a mail library API instead of raw headers

process.title: Administrative actions in [name] are not separately audited
process.desc: Changes made through admin functions (role changes, refunds, data exports, configuration) are not recorded with before/after values and who approved them.
controls: Dedicated audit trail for admin actions with old and new values
Four-eyes approval for the most critical actions

process.title: Users can deny transactions made through [name]
process.desc: Orders, payments or approvals are accepted without a reliable record of who confirmed them and when.
controls: Store who, what, when and from where for each transaction
Explicit confirmation step and receipts for important transactions

process.title: Requests through [name] cannot be traced across services
process.desc: Without correlation IDs passed between services, an investigation cannot follow one user action through the system.
controls: Generate and propagate a request/trace ID; log it everywhere
Central log search across services

process.title: Unsynchronised clocks make the timeline of [name] unreliable
process.desc: Servers without time synchronisation write timestamps that do not line up, so the order of events in an incident cannot be proven.
controls: NTP on all hosts; log in UTC with time zone
Monitor clock drift

process.title: Container of [name] runs as root or privileged
process.desc: Root or privileged containers, host mounts or added capabilities turn an application flaw into control of the node.
controls: Run as non-root with a read-only root file system
Drop all capabilities; no privileged mode or host mounts
Pod security standards (restricted)

process.title: Unverified or outdated base image for [name]
process.desc: Images built from unpinned public base images inherit known vulnerabilities or a tampered upstream image.
controls: Pin base images by digest; rebuild regularly
Scan images and verify signatures before deploy

process.title: Secrets for [name] in plain environment variables or baked into the image
process.desc: Environment variables and image layers are visible to anyone who can inspect the container, read crash dumps or pull the image.
controls: Mount secrets from a secret store at runtime
Never copy secrets into image layers; scan images for secrets

process.title: Admin portal [name] reachable from the internet
process.desc: Administrative interfaces exposed publicly are constantly attacked with stolen credentials and exploits.
controls: Restrict admin access to VPN / zero-trust access or allow-listed networks
Separate admin application from the public site

process.title: Sensitive admin actions in [name] without re-authentication
process.desc: A stolen or unattended admin session can change roles, export data or disable controls without being asked to prove identity again.
controls: Step-up authentication (MFA) for sensitive actions
Short admin session lifetimes

process.title: [name] trusts the mobile app to enforce rules
process.desc: Limits, prices and permissions are only checked in the app, so a modified app or direct API calls bypass them.
controls: Enforce every rule on the server
Treat the app like any other untrusted client

process.title: Old app versions keep using deprecated endpoints of [name]
process.desc: Legacy API versions stay online for old app installs and miss security fixes applied to the current version.
controls: Inventory and retire old API versions
Minimum supported app version enforced by the backend

process.title: Unsupported runtime or operating system under [name]
process.desc: End-of-life frameworks, runtimes or OS versions no longer receive security patches.
controls: Track end-of-life dates; upgrade plan per component
Isolate legacy systems that cannot be upgraded

process.title: Edge rules or functions for [name] changed through a compromised account
process.desc: Whoever controls the CDN configuration can redirect traffic, inject scripts or disable protection for the whole site.
controls: MFA and least privilege on CDN accounts; change approval
Alert on configuration changes

process.title: Function [name] hits concurrency limits
process.desc: Bursts of events use up account-wide concurrency, so this and unrelated functions are throttled.
controls: Reserved concurrency per critical function
Queue and back-pressure in front of functions

process.title: Batched GraphQL queries bypass login rate limits in [name]
process.desc: Aliases or batching let one HTTP request try hundreds of passwords or one-time codes, slipping past per-request rate limits.
controls: Rate-limit by operation, not by request
Disallow batching for authentication mutations

process.title: Messages processed twice or out of order by [name]
process.desc: At-least-once delivery without idempotency creates duplicate orders or payments; out-of-order processing applies old state.
controls: Idempotency keys and de-duplication
Version numbers or sequence checks on state changes

process.title: [name] abused to send spam
process.desc: Contact, invite or password-reset forms send email to any address, so attackers use your domain to spam until it is blocklisted.
controls: Rate limits and CAPTCHA on forms that send email
Do not include user-supplied text in automatic emails

process.title: Huge or numerous uploads exhaust storage of [name]
process.desc: Uploads without size and count limits fill disks or storage quotas.
controls: Per-user quotas and maximum file size
Stream to object storage instead of local disk

process.title: Uploaded files served by [name] run scripts in your domain
process.desc: HTML or SVG uploads served from the application's own domain execute JavaScript in users' sessions (stored XSS).
controls: Serve user files from a separate domain
Content-Disposition: attachment and correct content types
Sanitise or convert SVG/HTML

process.title: Payment status in [name] taken from the browser instead of the provider
process.desc: The order is marked as paid because of a success redirect or URL parameter, which a user can fake.
controls: Confirm payment server-to-server or via signed provider webhooks
Check amount and currency against the order

process.title: Account enumeration through login, reset or sign-up of [name]
process.desc: Different messages or timings reveal which emails or usernames have accounts, feeding phishing and credential stuffing.
controls: Identical responses and timing for existing and unknown accounts
Rate limits on these endpoints

process.title: Notifications from [name] reveal sensitive content on lock screens
process.desc: Push notifications include codes, balances or medical/personal details visible without unlocking the phone.
controls: Keep notification text generic; show details inside the app
Never send one-time codes with full context in notifications

process.title: Configuration or code of [name] writable by its own service account
process.desc: If the running service can modify its own binaries or config, any code-execution flaw becomes persistent.
controls: Separate deploy and runtime accounts; read-only application files
Integrity monitoring on config files

process.title: Disk full on the host stops [name]
process.desc: Logs, temporary files or uploads fill the disk and the service crashes or stops writing data.
controls: Log rotation and quotas; separate data volumes
Disk-usage alerts

process.title: Private API responses for [name] cached at the edge
process.desc: Responses that depend on the user are cached by the CDN and served to other users.
controls: Cache-Control: private/no-store on authenticated responses
Cache only explicitly public paths

process.title: Cache-busting requests bypass the CDN for [name]
process.desc: Random query strings or headers force every request through to the origin, defeating the CDN during an attack.
controls: Normalise or ignore unknown query parameters in the cache key
Rate limiting at the edge

datastore.title: Application connects to [name] with more rights than it needs
datastore.desc: The application's database account can change schemas, read every table or act as administrator, so an injection flaw becomes full data compromise.
controls: Separate accounts for migration, application and reporting
Grant only needed tables and operations
No shared admin accounts

datastore.title: [name] is directly reachable from another trust zone
datastore.desc: The data store accepts connections across a trust boundary, so it is exposed to attackers in that zone instead of only to the application.
controls: Only the owning service may connect (network rules, private endpoints)
Put a service with validation and authorization in front

datastore.title: Data in [name] changed outside the application
datastore.desc: Administrators, scripts or other services write directly to the store, bypassing validation, business rules and audit logging.
controls: Restrict direct write access; change data through reviewed scripts
Audit all direct changes

datastore.title: Cache poisoning in [name]
datastore.desc: Attackers get malicious or wrong values stored in a cache that other users or services then trust.
controls: Include all relevant inputs in cache keys
Validate data before caching; short TTLs for user-influenced data

datastore.title: Changes to [name] are not audited
datastore.desc: Changes to important data are not recorded with who made them and when, so unauthorised changes cannot be detected or attributed.
controls: Database audit logging or change-data-capture to a protected store
Record user and time on every change

datastore.title: Audit records in [name] can be rewritten by the people they record
datastore.desc: Administrators or the application can update or delete audit and transaction records, so evidence can be removed.
controls: Append-only / write-once storage for audit data
Separate ownership of audit logs from system administration

datastore.title: Sensitive data in [name] is not encrypted at rest
datastore.desc: Stolen disks, snapshots, backups or replicas expose the data directly.
controls: Storage or column-level encryption with managed keys
Encrypt backups and snapshots too

datastore.title: Passwords or secrets in [name] stored in a recoverable form
datastore.desc: Passwords are stored in plaintext or with fast hashes, or secrets are stored reversibly, so a database leak gives attackers working credentials.
controls: Passwords: Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt with per-user salt
Secrets: keep in a vault; store references, not values
Rotate credentials after any exposure

datastore.title: Storage bucket [name] is publicly accessible
datastore.desc: An object storage bucket or blob container allows anonymous listing or reading, exposing everything in it to anyone who finds the URL.
controls: Block public access at account level
Private endpoints and signed, expiring URLs
Automated checks for public buckets

datastore.title: [name] exposed to the internet without authentication
datastore.desc: Database, search or cache servers that listen on public addresses without authentication are found by scanners within hours and copied or wiped.
controls: Bind to private networks only; firewall rules
Always enable authentication, even internally
Continuous external exposure scanning
datastore.example: "Meow" attacks (2020): automated scripts wiped thousands of unsecured Elasticsearch and MongoDB databases.

datastore.title: Backups, exports or test copies of [name] are less protected than production
datastore.desc: Copies of production data in backup buckets, analytics exports or test environments lack the access controls of the original.
controls: Encrypt and restrict backups and exports
Masked or synthetic data in test environments
Track where copies of the data go

datastore.title: Personal data in [name] kept longer than needed
datastore.desc: Data that is no longer needed increases the damage of any breach and can violate data-protection law.
controls: Retention periods per data type with automatic deletion
Minimise stored fields

datastore.title: Ransomware or a compromised admin deletes [name] and its backups
datastore.desc: Attackers with administrative access encrypt or delete the data and the backups stored in the same account, making recovery impossible.
controls: Immutable or offline backups in a separate account
MFA and separate credentials for backup administration
Regularly test restores
datastore.example: Code Spaces (2014): an attacker with access to the AWS console deleted data, machines and backups; the company shut down.

datastore.title: Expensive queries or lock contention take [name] down
datastore.desc: Slow or deliberately heavy queries hold locks and connections so normal requests time out.
controls: Query timeouts and connection pool limits
Indexes for user-driven searches; read replicas
Rate-limit expensive operations

datastore.title: [name] runs out of storage
datastore.desc: Unbounded writes — uploads, logs, queues that are never drained — fill the disk and stop the data store.
controls: Quotas and size limits
Retention policies
Disk and queue-depth alerts

datastore.title: Pre-signed or shared links to [name] leak or live too long
datastore.desc: Download links with embedded signatures are shared, logged or cached and keep working for days, giving anyone who has them access to the file.
controls: Short expiry (minutes) for pre-signed URLs
Generate links per user after an authorization check

datastore.title: Public write access lets attackers change files in [name]
datastore.desc: Anyone can upload or overwrite objects — replacing downloads, scripts or website assets with malicious versions.
controls: Deny public write; only service roles can write
Versioning and object lock for important content

datastore.title: Unauthorised producers inject messages into [name]
datastore.desc: Any service or host with network access can publish to the queue or topic, so consumers process forged commands or events.
controls: Authentication and per-topic publish permissions
Sign messages that trigger important actions

datastore.title: Sensitive messages in [name] readable by many consumers
datastore.desc: Topics carry personal or payment data, and any consumer group or administrator can read the whole stream.
controls: Per-topic read permissions; separate topics for sensitive data
Encrypt sensitive payload fields

datastore.title: One credential can read every secret in [name]
datastore.desc: Applications or CI jobs use broad tokens, so compromising one of them exposes all secrets in the store.
controls: Per-application policies limited to their own secrets
Short-lived authentication (workload identity) instead of static tokens

datastore.title: Access to secrets in [name] is not audited
datastore.desc: Reads and changes of secrets are not logged, so a leaked token's use cannot be traced.
controls: Enable audit devices/logs; alert on unusual reads
Retain secret-access logs centrally

datastore.title: Logs in [name] contain personal data and are widely accessible
datastore.desc: Many engineers, tools and vendors can read logs that include user identifiers, IP addresses or request bodies.
controls: Minimise and pseudonymise logged personal data
Role-based access and retention limits for logs

datastore.title: Log flooding hides attacks or overloads [name]
datastore.desc: Attackers generate huge volumes of log events so real alerts are lost, storage fills up or the logging budget is exhausted.
controls: Rate-limit and sample noisy events
Alert on sudden log volume changes

datastore.title: Search results from [name] include documents the user may not see
datastore.desc: The search index contains everything, and permissions are not applied when querying, so searches reveal titles and snippets of restricted content.
controls: Filter search results by the user's permissions (document-level security)
Index only what each audience may see

datastore.title: Ransomware encrypts files on [name]
datastore.desc: Malware running with a user's or server's rights encrypts everything on mapped shares.
controls: Least-privilege share permissions
Immutable snapshots and offline backups
Detect mass file changes

datastore.title: Over-shared folders on [name] ("Everyone" permissions)
datastore.desc: Folders are readable by all staff or all authenticated users, exposing HR, finance or customer files.
controls: Review and remove broad permissions
Data-owner approval for access

datastore.title: Poisoned documents in [name] steer AI answers
datastore.desc: Attackers place content in the documents or embeddings used for retrieval (RAG), so the AI assistant gives manipulated answers or follows injected instructions.
controls: Control and review what gets indexed
Keep source attribution and trust levels per document
Separate tenants in vector stores

datastore.title: Card data stored in [name]
datastore.desc: Storing card numbers (PAN) makes the data store a high-value target and brings it into full PCI DSS scope.
controls: Store payment tokens from the provider instead of card numbers
If unavoidable: strong encryption, key separation, strict access

datastore.title: Deleted records in [name] leave no trace
datastore.desc: Hard deletes remove data without any history, so it cannot be shown who removed what.
controls: Soft delete or history tables for important data
Audit delete operations

datastore.title: Shared database accounts hide who changed [name]
datastore.desc: Several applications or people use the same database user, so changes cannot be attributed.
controls: One account per application and per person
Pass end-user identity into audit columns

datastore.title: Logs in [name] deleted before incidents are discovered
datastore.desc: Short retention means evidence is gone by the time a breach is noticed (often weeks or months later).
controls: Retention long enough for investigations (e.g. 12 months for security logs)
Archive to cheaper immutable storage

datastore.title: [name] returns other tenants' documents to the AI assistant
datastore.desc: A shared vector index without tenant or permission filters retrieves documents the current user may not see.
controls: Filter retrieval by tenant and user permissions
Separate indexes for separate tenants

datastore.title: Embeddings in [name] can reveal the original text
datastore.desc: Embedding vectors are treated as anonymous, but they can be inverted to recover much of the source content.
controls: Protect embeddings like the source data (access control, encryption)
Avoid embedding sensitive fields

datastore.title: Payee or bank details in [name] changed to redirect payments
datastore.desc: An attacker (or a fraudulent request) changes a supplier's or customer's bank account so payouts go to the attacker.
controls: Out-of-band verification for bank detail changes
Audit and alert on changes; delay first payment to new details

datastore.title: Sessions or tokens in [name] readable without authentication
datastore.desc: Caches inside the network often run without passwords or TLS, so anyone who reaches them can read sessions and cached data.
controls: Enable authentication and TLS on the cache
Network policies limiting access to the application

datastore.title: Cache stampede on [name] overloads the backend
datastore.desc: When popular entries expire together, many requests hit the database at once.
controls: Request coalescing / locking on refresh
Staggered expiry; serve stale while revalidating

datastore.title: Secrets store [name] unavailable stops all services
datastore.desc: If the store is down or sealed after a restart, every service that needs a secret fails to start.
controls: High-availability setup and tested unseal procedure
Short-lived caching of secrets in services

datastore.title: Secrets in [name] are never rotated
datastore.desc: Long-lived credentials stay valid for years, so any past leak is still usable.
controls: Automatic rotation; dynamic short-lived credentials where possible
Alert on secret age

datastore.title: Database [name] uses default or shared admin credentials
datastore.desc: Default, shared or well-known admin passwords give anyone who reaches the database full access.
controls: Unique, vaulted admin credentials; disable default accounts
Individual admin accounts with MFA via a bastion

datastore.title: Migrations or bulk jobs lock [name] in production
datastore.desc: Schema changes or large batch updates take table locks and stop the application.
controls: Online schema-change tools; run heavy jobs in batches
Test migrations on production-sized data

datastore.title: Listing enabled on bucket [name]
datastore.desc: Anyone allowed to list the bucket can enumerate every object name, then guess or fetch interesting files.
controls: Disable public list permissions
Unguessable object keys for user content

datastore.title: Objects in [name] deleted or all versions purged
datastore.desc: Without versioning or object lock, a compromised key or mistake permanently deletes data.
controls: Versioning and object lock (WORM) for important data
Separate account for backups; MFA delete

datastore.title: Messages in [name] cannot be traced to their producer
datastore.desc: Messages carry no producer identity or correlation ID, so a malicious or faulty message cannot be traced back.
controls: Include producer identity and correlation IDs in message metadata
Log publishes for sensitive topics

datastore.title: Malicious files planted on [name]
datastore.desc: Attackers place infected documents or shortcuts on shared folders that other users open.
controls: Malware scanning on shares
Read-only shares where users only consume content

datastore.title: Unvalidated document structure corrupts [name]
datastore.desc: Schemaless writes accept unexpected fields and types, breaking readers or smuggling data into places it should not be.
controls: Schema validation in the database or the data access layer
Reject unknown fields

datastore.title: Payment records in [name] can be edited without trace
datastore.desc: Amounts, statuses or refunds can be changed directly in the database, and nothing records who did it.
controls: Append-only ledger for payment events
Audit and alert on direct changes to payment tables

interactor.title: Phishing steals [name]'s credentials or session
interactor.desc: Fake login pages — including adversary-in-the-middle kits that relay one-time codes — capture passwords and session cookies.
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys)
Short sessions; bind sessions to device
User reporting of phishing

interactor.title: Privileged account of [name] taken over (no MFA)
interactor.desc: A privileged user signs in with a password only, so one leaked or guessed password gives an attacker administrative access.
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA for all privileged and remote access
Privileged access workstations / just-in-time admin rights
interactor.example: Change Healthcare (2024): attackers used stolen credentials on a remote-access portal that did not require MFA. Colonial Pipeline (2021): access was reportedly through a VPN account without MFA.

interactor.title: MFA fatigue: [name] approves a push prompt they did not start
interactor.desc: Attackers with a stolen password send repeated push notifications (often while posing as IT support) until the user accepts one.
controls: Number matching or FIDO2 instead of simple push approval
Limit and alert on repeated MFA prompts
interactor.example: Uber (2022): a contractor accepted a push after being flooded with prompts and contacted by the attacker posing as IT.

interactor.title: Credential stuffing with passwords leaked elsewhere
interactor.desc: Attackers try username/password pairs from other breaches or infostealer logs at scale; reused passwords let them in.
controls: MFA
Breached-password checks
Rate limiting and bot detection on login
interactor.example: Snowflake customer accounts (2024): attackers used credentials from infostealer malware against accounts without MFA and stole data from many companies.

interactor.title: Account recovery or SMS codes used to take over [name]'s account
interactor.desc: Weak password-reset flows, guessable security questions or SIM-swap attacks on SMS codes give attackers control of the account.
controls: Strong reset tokens and notification on reset
Avoid SMS as the only second factor
Extra verification for recovery of privileged accounts

interactor.title: API keys or tokens of [name] stolen and reused
interactor.desc: A partner's or client app's credentials leak (code, logs, device) and attackers call your API as that client.
controls: Short-lived tokens (OAuth2 client credentials) instead of static keys
Bind keys to IP or mTLS certificate; per-client scopes
Monitor and rotate keys

interactor.title: Supplier or partner [name] used as a way in
interactor.desc: Attackers compromise a vendor with access to your systems and use that trusted connection.
controls: Least-privilege, monitored vendor access
Separate network segment for third-party access
MFA and time-limited accounts for vendors
interactor.example: Target (2013): attackers entered with credentials stolen from a refrigeration/HVAC contractor and reached payment systems.

interactor.title: Bots pose as real users of [name] (fake sign-ups, scraping, enumeration)
interactor.desc: Anonymous access lets automated clients create fake accounts, scrape data or test which emails and phone numbers are registered.
controls: Rate limits and bot detection
Same response for existing and non-existing accounts
Protect sensitive business flows (sign-up, checkout)

interactor.title: Administrative access by [name] is exposed to the internet
interactor.desc: A privileged user reaches admin functions across a trust boundary without a VPN or zero-trust gateway, so the admin login is open to the whole internet.
controls: VPN or zero-trust access for admin interfaces
Admin endpoints on a separate host/network
MFA and IP restrictions

interactor.title: Actions by [name] cannot be attributed
interactor.desc: Connections from this entity are not authenticated, so the system cannot prove who performed an action.
controls: Authenticate connections
Record user, client and request IDs in audit logs

interactor.title: Shared accounts make actions by [name] untraceable
interactor.desc: Several people use the same account, so it is impossible to tell who did what.
controls: Personal accounts only; no shared credentials
Privileged access management with individual check-out

interactor.title: [name] disputes a transaction and there is no proof
interactor.desc: A customer or partner denies placing an order, approving a payment or receiving data, and the system has no reliable evidence.
controls: Signed receipts or confirmations for important transactions
Tamper-evident transaction logs with timestamps

interactor.title: Malware on [name]'s device steals sessions or data
interactor.desc: Infostealers and keyloggers on user or administrator devices capture passwords, session cookies and files.
controls: Managed, hardened devices for privileged users
Short sessions bound to device; re-authentication for sensitive actions
Endpoint detection and response
interactor.example: LastPass (2022): attackers installed a keylogger on a DevOps engineer's home computer via vulnerable third-party software and used the captured password to reach vault backups.

interactor.title: Insider misuse of [name]'s legitimate access
interactor.desc: Employees, support staff or administrators look up or export data they have access to but no business reason to see.
controls: Least privilege and need-to-know access
Audit and review access to sensitive records
Just-in-time access for support

interactor.title: Sensitive data left on shared or lost devices of [name]
interactor.desc: Cached pages, downloads and tokens in browser or app storage stay on shared, lost or stolen devices.
controls: Cache-Control: no-store for sensitive pages
Keep tokens out of local storage; short sessions
Device encryption / mobile app data protection

interactor.title: Help desk tricked into resetting [name]'s password or MFA
interactor.desc: An attacker calls or messages support pretending to be the user and gets the password or MFA device reset.
controls: Strong identity verification for resets (call-back, manager approval, ID check)
Extra scrutiny for privileged accounts; notify the user on reset
interactor.example: MGM Resorts (2023): attackers impersonated an employee in a call to the IT help desk and gained access that led to a major outage.

interactor.title: Consent phishing: [name] authorises a malicious app
interactor.desc: Users are tricked into granting a third-party OAuth app access to their mail or files, giving attackers long-lived tokens without a password.
controls: Admin approval for third-party app consent
Review and revoke risky app grants

interactor.title: Secrets extracted from the [name] app
interactor.desc: API keys, tokens or endpoints embedded in the app binary are recovered by decompiling it.
controls: No long-lived secrets in apps; per-user tokens from the backend
App attestation for backend calls

interactor.title: Modified app or emulator impersonates the official [name] client
interactor.desc: Repackaged apps or scripts call your API as if they were the official app, bypassing client-side checks.
controls: Server-side enforcement of all rules
App attestation (Play Integrity / App Attest) for sensitive calls

interactor.title: Device identity of [name] can be cloned
interactor.desc: Devices share the same key or use guessable identifiers, so one extracted key lets attackers impersonate every device.
controls: Unique per-device keys or certificates, stored in secure hardware
Revocation per device

interactor.title: [name] receives more data than it needs
interactor.desc: Integrations send full records to partners when only a few fields are required, increasing exposure and breaching data-minimisation rules.
controls: Partner-specific APIs/views with only the needed fields
Data processing agreements and periodic review

interactor.title: Approvals by [name] are given outside the system
interactor.desc: Changes are approved in chat or email instead of in the tool, so there is no reliable record linking approval to change.
controls: Approvals recorded in the system of record
Link change records to approvers

interactor.title: Automated client [name] acts with a person's identity
interactor.desc: Scripts or integrations use a person's credentials, so automated actions look like human ones and cannot be separated.
controls: Dedicated service identities for automation
Mark automated actions in audit logs

interactor.title: Partner [name] disputes data it sent or received
interactor.desc: Without signed messages or delivery receipts, a partner can deny having sent or received an order or file.
controls: Message signing and acknowledgements for B2B exchanges
Keep exchanged messages with timestamps

interactor.title: Data shown to [name] exposed via screen sharing or onlookers
interactor.desc: Support and operations staff show customer data on shared screens, calls or in public places.
controls: Mask sensitive fields by default; reveal on demand with logging
Privacy screens and screen-sharing guidance

interactor.title: [name] copies data to personal email, cloud drives or AI tools
interactor.desc: Users move company or customer data into unsanctioned services where it is no longer protected or deletable.
controls: Data loss prevention for uploads and email
Provide approved tools, including approved AI assistants

interactor.title: Exports made by [name] stay on laptops and in inboxes
interactor.desc: CSV and report exports leave the system's access controls and retention.
controls: Limit and log exports; watermark reports
Expiry for shared export links

interactor.title: Device [name] connects to a server it does not authenticate
interactor.desc: Devices accept any server certificate or none, so a spoofed backend can send commands or firmware.
controls: Pin or validate the server certificate on the device
Mutual TLS between device and backend

interactor.title: Device [name] leaks data when sold, recycled or lost
interactor.desc: Credentials and data remain on devices that leave the organisation.
controls: Secure factory reset and remote wipe
Revoke device credentials at decommissioning

interactor.title: Compromised external identity provider [name] signs in as anyone
interactor.desc: Federation means you trust every login the provider asserts; if it is compromised, attackers can log in as any of your users.
controls: Limit which domains/tenants are trusted
Monitor federated logins; MFA enforced on your side for admins

interactor.title: Accounts from [name] are linked by email address alone
interactor.desc: Linking an external login to a local account just because the email matches lets someone who controls an unverified email address take over the account.
controls: Link accounts on the provider's stable subject ID
Require verified email and explicit linking by the user

interactor.title: Fake payment notifications pretending to come from [name]
interactor.desc: Forged callbacks or emails claim that a payment succeeded or a refund is due.
controls: Verify provider signatures; confirm status via the provider API
Never act on emailed payment confirmations alone

interactor.title: Payment provider [name] receives more customer data than needed
interactor.desc: Full customer profiles are sent where only an amount and reference are required.
controls: Send only fields the provider needs
Data processing agreement and review of shared fields

interactor.title: App [name] stores tokens or data insecurely on the device
interactor.desc: Tokens and personal data in plain files, shared preferences or logs are readable on rooted devices and in backups.
controls: Use the platform keystore/keychain for secrets
Exclude sensitive data from backups and logs

interactor.title: Logins via [name] cannot be matched to your own logs
interactor.desc: Your logs do not keep the provider's user and session identifiers, so a suspicious login there cannot be followed into your system.
controls: Log the IdP subject, session ID and authentication method
Keep IdP sign-in logs for the same period

interactor.title: Chargebacks via [name] cannot be contested
interactor.desc: Without evidence of authentication (3-D Secure), delivery and customer consent, disputed payments are lost.
controls: Keep authentication results, delivery proof and order history per payment
Use strong customer authentication where available

infrastructure.title: Default or shared credentials on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Devices, appliances and platforms shipped with default admin passwords — or one password shared across many devices — are taken over by automated scanning.
controls: Change defaults at install; unique credentials per device
Disable unused services (telnet, default admin UI)
infrastructure.example: Mirai (2016): malware logged into hundreds of thousands of IoT devices with default passwords and used them for record DDoS attacks.

infrastructure.title: Rogue device impersonates [name]
infrastructure.desc: A device spoofs this host's IP, MAC or hostname to receive traffic or join the network as a trusted machine.
controls: Network access control (802.1X), device certificates
Alert on duplicate addresses

infrastructure.title: Firmware or system configuration of [name] changed without detection
infrastructure.desc: Exposed management ports or missing secure boot let attackers modify firmware or configuration and persist.
controls: Secure boot; signed firmware updates
Configuration baselines with drift detection
Restrict management access

infrastructure.title: Logs from [name] are not collected centrally
infrastructure.desc: Host, network and cloud control-plane logs stay where an attacker can disable or delete them.
controls: Forward logs to a central SIEM in real time
Alert when logging is disabled or stops

infrastructure.title: Cloud instance credentials of [name] stolen via the metadata service
infrastructure.desc: Code running on the host — or an SSRF flaw — reads temporary cloud credentials from the instance metadata endpoint.
controls: Require IMDSv2 / metadata protection
Least-privilege instance roles
Block metadata access from containers that do not need it
infrastructure.example: Capital One (2019): credentials from the EC2 metadata service were used to read S3 data.

infrastructure.title: Secrets in plaintext on disks, images or snapshots of [name]
infrastructure.desc: Configuration files, scripts, VM images and snapshots contain passwords and keys readable by anyone with access to them.
controls: Secret manager; inject at runtime
Scan images and repositories for secrets
Encrypt disks and snapshots

infrastructure.title: Lost or stolen [name] exposes its data
infrastructure.desc: Laptops, devices and disks that leave the building — lost, stolen or decommissioned — still contain readable data.
controls: Full-disk encryption
Remote wipe; secure decommissioning

infrastructure.title: Single instance of [name] with no redundancy
infrastructure.desc: One host, zone or network path failing — or being attacked — takes the whole service down.
controls: Redundancy across zones
Health checks and automatic failover
Tested recovery procedures

infrastructure.title: Other workloads exhaust shared resources of [name]
infrastructure.desc: Neighbouring workloads on the same host, cluster or account consume CPU, memory or quotas.
controls: Resource limits and reservations
Separate accounts or clusters for critical workloads

infrastructure.title: Management interface of [name] reachable from an untrusted network
infrastructure.desc: SSH, RDP, Kubernetes API, hypervisor or admin consoles are reachable across a trust boundary and are attacked with stolen credentials and exploits.
controls: Management only via VPN/bastion/zero-trust access
MFA on all administrative access
Allow-list source addresses

infrastructure.title: Unpatched OS or services on [name] allow remote takeover
infrastructure.desc: Known vulnerabilities in the operating system or exposed services are exploited to run code with high privileges.
controls: Patch management with SLAs
Minimise exposed services
Vulnerability scanning

infrastructure.title: Container escape from [name] to the host
infrastructure.desc: Privileged containers, mounted host paths or kernel flaws let code inside a container take over the host and its other containers.
controls: No privileged containers or host mounts
Run as non-root; seccomp/AppArmor
Patch the host kernel and runtime

infrastructure.title: Flat network lets attackers move from [name] to other systems
infrastructure.desc: Once one machine is compromised, nothing stops connections to databases, admin systems and other hosts.
controls: Network segmentation and default-deny between zones
Monitor east-west traffic
infrastructure.example: Target (2013): attackers moved from a vendor portal to point-of-sale systems inside the network.

infrastructure.title: Exploitable VPN or edge appliance [name]
infrastructure.desc: Internet-facing VPNs, gateways and firewalls are prime targets; pre-authentication vulnerabilities give attackers a foothold inside the network.
controls: Patch within days for edge devices; subscribe to vendor advisories
Restrict management interfaces; monitor for integrity changes
Terminate sessions after patching
infrastructure.example: Ivanti Connect Secure (2024, CVE-2023-46805 + CVE-2024-21887) was mass-exploited for unauthenticated command execution. Citrix Bleed (2023, CVE-2023-4966) leaked session tokens that bypassed MFA.

infrastructure.title: DNS for [name] hijacked through the registrar or DNS provider account
infrastructure.desc: Taking over the DNS or registrar account lets attackers point your domains at their servers and obtain valid certificates.
controls: MFA and restricted access on registrar/DNS accounts; registry lock
Monitor DNS record changes and certificate issuance (CT logs)

infrastructure.title: Dangling DNS records allow subdomain takeover
infrastructure.desc: Records still point at deleted cloud resources (apps, buckets, CDN endpoints), which attackers can claim to serve content on your subdomain.
controls: Remove DNS records when resources are deleted
Scan for dangling CNAMEs regularly

infrastructure.title: Web cache deception or poisoning on [name]
infrastructure.desc: The CDN caches personalised pages under static-looking URLs, or caches responses influenced by unkeyed headers, serving them to other users.
controls: Cache only explicitly cacheable paths; respect Cache-Control
Normalise and key on all inputs that change the response

infrastructure.title: Overly permissive Kubernetes RBAC on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Service accounts or users have cluster-admin, wildcard or secrets-read permissions, so one compromised pod controls the cluster.
controls: Least-privilege roles per namespace; no wildcard verbs
Disable automounting service account tokens where not needed

infrastructure.title: Kubernetes secrets on [name] readable by too many
infrastructure.desc: Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted at rest, and readable by broad roles or anyone with node access.
controls: Encryption at rest for secrets (KMS provider)
External secret store; restrict get/list on secrets

infrastructure.title: Long-lived cloud access keys for [name] leak
infrastructure.desc: Static access keys in laptops, CI systems or repositories are copied and used from anywhere.
controls: Short-lived role-based credentials (SSO, workload identity)
Key age alerts and automatic rotation
Secret scanning

infrastructure.title: Disk snapshots or images of [name] shared publicly
infrastructure.desc: Snapshots, AMIs or images are made public or shared with other accounts, exposing their full disk contents.
controls: Block public sharing at account level
Encrypt snapshots with customer-managed keys

infrastructure.title: Directory service [name] compromised (Kerberoasting, weak service accounts)
infrastructure.desc: Service accounts with weak passwords and broad rights can be cracked offline from Kerberos tickets, leading to domain-wide control.
controls: Long random passwords or managed service accounts
Tiered administration; monitor for ticket requests from unusual hosts

infrastructure.title: Unpatched mail server [name] exploited
infrastructure.desc: Internet-facing mail servers are frequently exploited for remote code execution and mailbox access.
controls: Patch quickly or move to a managed mail service
Restrict admin and web endpoints
infrastructure.example: Microsoft Exchange ProxyLogon (2021, CVE-2021-26855): mass exploitation of on-premises Exchange servers.

infrastructure.title: Unsigned firmware updates on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Devices accept firmware updates that are not signed or are downloaded over plain HTTP, so attackers can install their own firmware.
controls: Signed firmware verified on the device
Updates over TLS; anti-rollback

infrastructure.title: Debug ports on [name] give a root shell
infrastructure.desc: UART, JTAG or test interfaces left enabled let anyone with physical access read firmware and secrets or take control.
controls: Disable or lock debug interfaces in production
Store keys in secure elements

infrastructure.title: [name] can be abused to amplify DDoS attacks
infrastructure.desc: Open UDP services (DNS resolvers, NTP, memcached) answer spoofed requests with much larger responses aimed at a victim.
controls: Do not expose UDP services to the internet; disable recursion for public DNS
Source address validation (BCP 38)
infrastructure.example: GitHub (2018): a 1.35 Tbps attack used publicly exposed memcached servers as amplifiers.

infrastructure.title: Manual changes to [name] bypass infrastructure-as-code
infrastructure.desc: Hand-made changes drift from the reviewed configuration and silently undo security settings.
controls: Infrastructure as code with review; restrict console write access
Drift detection and alerts

infrastructure.title: Firewall or security group rules on [name] opened too widely
infrastructure.desc: "Temporary" allow-any rules or 0.0.0.0/0 exposures remain in place long after they were needed.
controls: Rule review and expiry dates; least-open rules
Automated checks for wide-open rules

infrastructure.title: No admission control on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Anyone who can deploy can run privileged or unverified workloads, because no central policy checks them.
controls: Admission policies (e.g. Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper) for images, privileges and labels
Signed images only

infrastructure.title: Tampered VM or container images deployed to [name]
infrastructure.desc: Images pulled from public registries or shared accounts without signature checks may contain backdoors.
controls: Private registry; verify image signatures
Approved base images only

infrastructure.title: Cloud control-plane activity for [name] not logged
infrastructure.desc: API activity logs (e.g. CloudTrail / Activity Log) are disabled, short-lived or writable by the admins they record.
controls: Organisation-wide control-plane logging to a separate account
Alert when logging is changed

infrastructure.title: Shared admin accounts on [name]
infrastructure.desc: The team shares one admin or root login, so actions cannot be tied to a person.
controls: Individual admin accounts; vault shared break-glass credentials
Session recording for privileged access

infrastructure.title: No network flow logs for [name]
infrastructure.desc: Without flow logs, connections to and from the system cannot be reconstructed after an incident.
controls: Enable VPC/firewall flow logs for critical segments
Retain and centralise them

infrastructure.title: Expired certificate or domain takes [name] offline
infrastructure.desc: TLS certificates or domain registrations that are not renewed in time cause sudden outages.
controls: Automated certificate renewal (ACME)
Expiry monitoring for certificates and domains
infrastructure.example: Microsoft Teams (February 2020): an expired authentication certificate caused a multi-hour outage.

infrastructure.title: Cloud quotas or account suspension take [name] offline
infrastructure.desc: Hitting service quotas, unpaid bills or an abuse-triggered suspension stops everything in the account.
controls: Quota monitoring and increases ahead of growth
Billing alerts; separate accounts for critical workloads

infrastructure.title: ARP or DHCP spoofing on the network of [name]
infrastructure.desc: An attacker on the local network answers ARP or DHCP requests and routes traffic through their machine.
controls: Dynamic ARP inspection and DHCP snooping on switches
Encrypt traffic even on internal networks

infrastructure.title: Rogue Wi-Fi access point imitates [name]
infrastructure.desc: An "evil twin" network with the same name captures logins and traffic from devices that connect automatically.
controls: WPA3-Enterprise with certificate validation
Wireless intrusion detection

infrastructure.title: VPN [name] accepts passwords without MFA
infrastructure.desc: One phished or reused password gives full network access.
controls: MFA for every VPN login; remove legacy accounts
Device certificates or posture checks

infrastructure.title: VPN users of [name] can reach the whole network
infrastructure.desc: After connecting, users and compromised laptops reach every internal system, not just what they need.
controls: Per-group access policies / zero-trust network access
Segment sensitive systems behind additional controls

infrastructure.title: Too many domain admin accounts on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Privileged directory accounts are numerous and used for everyday work, so any compromised workstation can expose them.
controls: Minimise domain admins; separate admin accounts
Privileged access workstations and tiering

infrastructure.title: Password hashes extracted from [name] (DCSync / NTDS.dit)
infrastructure.desc: Attackers with replication rights or disk access copy all password hashes and reuse them.
controls: Restrict replication rights; monitor DCSync requests
Protect domain controller backups

infrastructure.title: Mail server [name] is an open relay
infrastructure.desc: The server accepts mail for any recipient from anyone, so it is used for spam and phishing in your name.
controls: Relay only for authenticated users and own domains
Regular open-relay checks

infrastructure.title: Mailboxes on [name] accessible through legacy protocols without MFA
infrastructure.desc: IMAP, POP or basic-auth protocols bypass MFA and are used for password spraying and mailbox theft.
controls: Disable legacy/basic authentication
Conditional access for mail clients

infrastructure.title: Same local admin password on [name] and other machines
infrastructure.desc: A shared local administrator password lets an attacker who compromises one machine log into all others (pass-the-hash).
controls: Unique, rotated local admin passwords (LAPS)
Restrict local admin logons over the network

infrastructure.title: No endpoint detection or integrity monitoring on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Malware and persistence mechanisms (new services, scheduled tasks) go unnoticed.
controls: Endpoint detection and response
File integrity monitoring on critical servers

infrastructure.title: Origin behind [name] reachable directly, bypassing CDN and WAF
infrastructure.desc: If the origin server accepts traffic from anywhere, attackers skip the WAF, rate limits and DDoS protection.
controls: Allow only CDN IP ranges or authenticated origin pulls
Keep the origin address private

infrastructure.title: Configuration changes on [name] are not tracked
infrastructure.desc: Network device or appliance configs are changed without versioning, so nobody can tell who opened a rule or when.
controls: Configuration backups with diffs and change tickets
Syslog of configuration commands to a central store

flow.title: Traffic on [name] can be read on the network
flow.desc: The flow is not encrypted and leaves its trust zone, so anyone on the network path can capture credentials and data.
controls: TLS 1.2+ (or mTLS) on every connection
HSTS; disable plaintext fallbacks

flow.title: Traffic on [name] modified in transit (man-in-the-middle)
flow.desc: Without transport encryption and integrity, an attacker on the path can alter requests and responses.
controls: TLS with certificate validation; mTLS between services
Message signing for critical payloads

flow.title: Unauthenticated messages accepted on [name] across a trust boundary
flow.desc: The receiver cannot verify who sent the data, so attackers in the other zone can inject their own requests or messages.
controls: Mutual TLS or signed tokens on the flow
Validate sender identity before processing

flow.title: Sensitive data on [name] sent in cleartext
flow.desc: The flow connects to a component that holds personal data, credentials or other sensitive data, but it is not encrypted.
controls: Encrypt in transit
Send only the fields that are needed

flow.title: Webhook or queue messages on [name] accepted without signature check
flow.desc: Anyone who can reach the endpoint or queue can post fake events (payments, status changes) because messages are not verified.
controls: Verify HMAC signatures or use mTLS
Check timestamps/nonces to reject replays
Restrict who can publish to the queue

flow.title: TLS certificate validation disabled for [name]
flow.desc: Client code skips certificate checks (often to work around test certificates), which silently allows man-in-the-middle attacks.
controls: Never disable verification in production code
Use a private CA for internal certificates
Tests that fail on invalid certificates

flow.title: Captured requests on [name] can be replayed
flow.desc: Requests carry no timestamp, nonce or one-time token, so a captured request (payment, approval) can be sent again.
controls: Nonces/timestamps with short validity
Idempotency keys for one-time actions

flow.title: Tokens or personal data in URLs of [name]
flow.desc: Values in query strings end up in proxy and server logs, browser history and Referer headers.
controls: Send secrets in headers or POST bodies
Referrer-Policy; avoid personal data in URLs

flow.title: Outdated TLS settings on [name] allow downgrade or weak encryption
flow.desc: Old protocol versions and cipher suites allow downgrade attacks and remove forward secrecy, so recorded traffic may be decrypted later.
controls: TLS 1.2+ only (prefer 1.3), ECDHE suites
Regular TLS configuration scans

flow.title: Flooding of [name] from an anonymous source
flow.desc: Anyone can send traffic on this flow into another trust zone, which makes request floods easy.
controls: Rate limiting and DDoS protection at the edge
Patch servers for protocol-level DoS flaws
Autoscaling with limits
flow.example: HTTP/2 Rapid Reset (2023, CVE-2023-44487): rapidly opening and cancelling streams produced record DDoS attacks against major providers.

flow.title: Slow-request attacks hold connections on [name] open (Slowloris)
flow.desc: Clients send requests very slowly to occupy all connection slots on the receiving server.
controls: Header/body timeouts and per-client connection limits
Reverse proxy or load balancer in front

flow.title: [name] depends on a single network path or provider
flow.desc: If the link, DNS, certificate or upstream provider fails, the flow stops and nothing takes over.
controls: Redundant paths/providers for critical flows
Monitor certificate expiry and DNS
Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers

flow.title: WebSocket connection [name] accepted from any website
flow.desc: The server does not check the Origin of WebSocket handshakes, so a malicious page can open a connection with the user's cookies (cross-site WebSocket hijacking).
controls: Validate the Origin header on handshake
Token-based authentication for WebSocket sessions

flow.title: Tokens on [name] leak through redirects, URLs or referrers
flow.desc: Access tokens or authorization codes travel in URL fragments or query strings, where browser history, logs and Referer headers expose them.
controls: Authorization code flow with PKCE; no implicit flow
Tokens in headers or POST bodies; strict Referrer-Policy

flow.title: Email on [name] sent without enforced TLS
flow.desc: Opportunistic STARTTLS can be stripped, so messages travel in plaintext between mail servers.
controls: MTA-STS and TLS reporting
Encrypt sensitive content end-to-end instead of relying on transport

flow.title: Broker connection [name] without TLS or authentication
flow.desc: MQTT, AMQP or Kafka connections run in plaintext or anonymously inside the network, exposing messages and allowing anyone to connect.
controls: TLS and per-client credentials on brokers
Network policies limiting who can reach the broker

flow.title: Administration over [name] uses weak protocols
flow.desc: Telnet, VNC without TLS or legacy RDP settings expose administrator credentials and sessions.
controls: SSH/RDP with modern encryption and network-level authentication
Access only through a bastion or VPN

flow.title: Database connection [name] not encrypted inside the network
flow.desc: Internal database traffic is assumed safe, but anyone on the network path can read queries, results and credentials.
controls: Require TLS on database connections; verify server certificates

flow.title: HTTP request smuggling between proxy and server on [name]
flow.desc: Front-end and back-end servers disagree on where a request ends, letting attackers prepend requests to other users' traffic.
controls: Use HTTP/2 end-to-end or consistent parsing; reject ambiguous requests
Keep proxies and servers updated

flow.title: Missing timeouts on [name] let a slow dependency block callers
flow.desc: Calls without timeouts wait indefinitely, tying up threads and connections until the caller fails too.
controls: Timeouts on every outbound call
Circuit breakers and bulkheads

flow.title: Retry storms on [name] turn a hiccup into an outage
flow.desc: Clients retry immediately and repeatedly, multiplying load on a struggling service.
controls: Exponential backoff with jitter; retry budgets
Honour Retry-After and rate-limit responses

flow.title: Backlog on [name] delays critical events
flow.desc: A slow consumer or a flood of low-priority messages delays important ones (payments, security alerts).
controls: Separate queues/topics by priority
Alert on consumer lag

flow.title: Oversized payloads on [name] exhaust the receiver
flow.desc: Requests or messages without size limits consume memory and CPU when parsed.
controls: Maximum body/message size at gateway and broker
Streaming parsers for large data

flow.title: Replayed webhook events on [name] processed again
flow.desc: A captured, correctly signed event is sent again and triggers the same action twice.
controls: Check signed timestamps and reject old events
Store processed event IDs

flow.title: Secret in the webhook URL for [name] leaks
flow.desc: Webhook URLs with secrets in the path or query end up in logs, tickets and screenshots.
controls: Signature headers instead of secrets in URLs
Rotate webhook secrets

flow.title: Tokens on [name] accepted by the wrong service
flow.desc: A token issued for one API is replayed to another that does not check the audience.
controls: Validate audience (aud) and issuer on every service
Narrow scopes per API

flow.title: LDAP bind on [name] sends passwords in cleartext
flow.desc: Simple binds over plain LDAP expose user and service passwords on the network.
controls: LDAPS or StartTLS required; disable plain simple binds
Use service accounts with minimal rights

flow.title: Phishing links or malicious attachments arrive via [name]
flow.desc: Inbound email is the most common way malware and credential phishing reach users.
controls: Mail filtering, sandboxing and link rewriting
Mark external email; user reporting button

flow.title: Email on [name] auto-forwarded outside the organisation
flow.desc: Attackers with mailbox access create forwarding rules that silently copy mail to them.
controls: Block automatic external forwarding
Alert on new forwarding rules

flow.title: Remote admin session on [name] hijacked
flow.desc: Disconnected or unattended privileged sessions are taken over by another user on the host.
controls: Session time-outs and logoff of disconnected sessions
Restrict who can connect to admin hosts

flow.title: Brute force on [name] locks out administrators
flow.desc: Account lockout policies let attackers lock admins out on purpose during an incident.
controls: Rate limiting and MFA instead of hard lockouts
Admin access only from trusted networks

flow.title: Database credentials for [name] sit in plain connection strings
flow.desc: Connection strings with passwords are stored in config files, environment dumps and logs.
controls: Pull credentials from a secret store; use IAM/managed identities
Never log connection strings

flow.title: Any service can open a connection like [name] to the database
flow.desc: The database port is reachable from many networks, so any compromised host can try to connect.
controls: Network rules allowing only the owning service
Private endpoints

flow.title: Messages on [name] altered at the broker or in transit
flow.desc: Without message-level integrity, anyone with broker access can change events (amounts, statuses) before consumers read them.
controls: Sign critical messages; verify in consumers
Restrict broker admin access

flow.title: Missing security headers on [name] (HSTS, CSP)
flow.desc: Without HSTS the first connection can be downgraded to HTTP; without CSP, injected scripts run freely.
controls: HSTS with preload; Content-Security-Policy
X-Content-Type-Options and frame-ancestors
